title: The Bavan Akhri's heart
hook: cleverness without the Name goes nowhere, says one letter of the Bavan Akhri (Gauri, ang 260)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bavan Akhri, Guru Arjan's fifty-two letters: an acrostic where each letter opens a lesson, and the Guru is mother and father. Your line was the letters again.

Can a person know a great deal and still miss the point? Maybe you've met one: the uncle who can win any argument at the table and never seems happy, the friend who's read everything about love and can't keep a friendship going. Knowing isn't the problem. Something is missing from the middle of it. The Bavan Akhri hands that lesson to one letter of the alphabet.
screen: `KNOWING A GREAT DEAL.` → `STILL MISSING THE POINT.` → `ONE LETTER'S LESSON.`

segments.voice: The letter is sassa, the S sound in Gurmukhi. Its stanza, paraphrased: Sassa: give up your cleverness, you who don't understand. The Lord is not won over by clever tricks or by giving orders. You may try a thousand kinds of cleverness, but not one of them will go with you. Hear the play on the letter: sassa opens with siaanap, cleverness. The alphabet itself is teaching. A few days back, Guru Amar Das told the restless mind that no one finds the Lord through cleverness. Guru Arjan's stanza takes a different turn: it asks what your cleverness can carry with you. First, what the stanza doesn't say. It doesn't say learning is bad. This is a hymn built out of the alphabet. Guru Arjan isn't against letters, only a certain use of them. Second, the two things named: clever tricks and commands. Being smart enough to get your way, and powerful enough to order it. Both are ways of staying in control, and the Lord isn't won by either. Third, the thousand kinds. Multiply your cleverness as far as you like; not one goes with you. That's the stanza's measure: not how much you know, but what goes with you. In Sikh teaching, what goes with you is the Name. So learning is welcome, and letters are a gift. But learning without the Name at its center is like a beautifully built house with nobody living in it. What the Guru asks isn't less knowledge. It's knowledge with a heart: learned humbly, held loosely, pointed toward the Name.
screen: `SASSA: GIVE UP YOUR CLEVERNESS.` · `NOT AGAINST LETTERS, AGAINST A USE.` · `A THOUSAND KINDS, NONE GOES WITH YOU.` · `KNOWLEDGE WITH THE NAME AT ITS CENTER.` · then, large: `THE BAVAN AKHRI'S HEART.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you're learning right now, a skill for work, a language, a recipe, a hymn, and ask it one quiet question: not what will you get me, but what are you for, who could you serve? Let an answer come, even a small one, and hold it for a few breaths, with Waheguru if you pray.
The Bavan Akhri's heart. Sassa's lesson: give up your cleverness; a thousand kinds of it won't go with you, but the Name will. Today's word.
Your line: learning with heart. Knowledge is welcome; the Name is what goes with you. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs read the Bavan Akhri in the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teachers turn to stanzas like this one when they speak of learning held with humility and pointed toward the Name.

chat.says: Does Guru Arjan's sassa stanza mean that studying and learning are bad?
options: No. It's against a use of cleverness; learning is welcome, but only the Name goes with you.
Yes. It says letters and books pull you away, so it's best to stop studying.
No. It says enough cleverness and learning will win the Lord over in the end.
chat.meaning: The sassa stanza isn't against letters: clever tricks and commands don't win the Lord, and a thousand kinds of cleverness won't go with you.
